memoryText: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Acts 16:31 slowly, several times, and say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
A Philippian jailer, trembling after an earthquake, asks Paul and Silas the most important question: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” This is their answer.

“Believe.” To believe is more than agreeing with facts. It is to trust, to rely on, to put your weight on. The jailer is not told to do a task, but to trust a person.

“In the Lord Jesus.” The object of faith is Jesus, the Lord who died and rose. He is the only Savior. “Lord” means the one who rules, and “Jesus” means the one who saves. To believe in him is to trust him as both.

“And you will be saved.” The promise is certain. Not “might be” or “could be.” Saved from sin, from judgment, and from death, and saved into life with God.

“You and your household.” The promise is for the jailer and extends to his family, who also heard the word and believed. It reminds us that God often works through families, and that faith in the head of a home opens the door to the gospel for the rest.

When you wonder what you must do to be saved or how to tell someone else, say this verse. It is the simplest summary of the gospel in the Bible.
weekInReview: This week you prayed Psalm 117, the shortest call to the nations. You followed the first journey to its end in Lystra and Derbe, where Paul was mistaken for a god and then stoned. At the Jerusalem Council, you saw the apostles decide that Gentiles are saved by grace, as Jews are, and you heard James cite Amos 9 about the rebuilding of David’s tent. You watched the second journey carry the gospel to Europe: Lydia’s heart was opened, and a jailer asked what he must do to be saved. You heard Paul preach to the Areopagus in Athens, you saw the Bereans search the Scriptures, and you spent three years in Ephesus, where the word prevailed mightily and magic books burned.
reflectionQuestions: The Jerusalem Council concluded that we are saved “through the grace of the Lord Jesus.” How do you tend to add to grace, and what would it mean to rest in it?
Lydia’s heart was opened by the Lord. Reflect on the moment God opened your heart. What did you notice then, and how has it changed you?
Paul preached differently to the Jews in Thessalonica and the philosophers in Athens. Who is your audience, and how might you meet them where they are while keeping the message of Christ the same?
prayerPrompts: Say with the jailer, “I believe in the Lord Jesus,” and mean it.
Pray for your household or those closest to you.
